Lesson 6

Who Is at Risk? Protecting the Household

High Blood Pressure and Diabetes · Lesson 6

Who Is at Risk? Protecting the Household

A flipchart for Care Group meetings. Show the picture side to the group. Turn to the text side to read the story, the questions and the messages.

  • Next and Back, or a swipe, turn the page.
  • Tap a picture to make it fill the screen.
  • Text shows what the facilitator reads. Picture goes back.

Lesson 6 at a glance

90 minutes. Bring the attendance registers and this flipchart. No materials are needed from the Activity Leader.

SectionMinutes
1. Game: The Mirror5
2. Attendance and troubleshooting10
3 and 4. Story and questions Picture 6.110
5. Risks We Cannot Change and Risks We Can Change Picture 6.210
6. Protect the Whole Household Picture 6.310
7. Activity: Step Forward, and the Household Check Plan15
8. Discuss barriers10

10. Request commitments10
Total90

Before the pictures

Game: The Mirror. In pairs, one person moves slowly and the other copies her like a mirror. Change roles. Say: “Children are the mirrors of the adults in the house.”

Recall Lesson 5. Blood pressure has two numbers. The aim for most adults is below 140 over 90. Before food, the aim for sugar is 7 or below. Ask for your numbers and keep your card.

Commitments. Ask: “What was your commitment at the last lesson? Have you been able to keep it?”

After the pictures

Step Forward. Everyone stands in one line. Say: “If a sentence is true for anyone in your household, take one step forward. You do not need to say who it is.”

  • Someone in my household is 40 years old or more.
  • Someone in my household has a parent, a brother or a sister with BP or sugar disease.
  • Someone in my household adds salt at the table, or we use two or more seasoning cubes in one pot.
  • Someone in my household takes a sweet drink on most days.
  • Someone in my household sits for most of the day at work.
  • Someone in my household has a big belly.
  • Someone in my household smokes, or takes alcohol on most days.
  • An adult in my household has not had a blood pressure check this year.

Say: “Almost all of us have moved forward. Every household has risks. This is not a reason for shame.” Read the sentences again. Ask each time: “Can a household change this?” When the group says yes, everyone steps back. The first two cannot be changed.

Household check plan. In pairs, each person counts the adults in her household, says which have not been checked this year, and chooses one to take first.

Discuss barriers. Ask: “Is there anything that might prevent the adults in your household from going for a check?”

Request commitments. Ask: “Based on what you have heard today, what commitment will you make?” Each person chooses. Do not press anyone who is not ready.

Picture 6.1Story: Abena’s Turn

Picture 6.1 · text sideStory: Abena’s Turn

Read the story aloud.

Abena goes with her parents to the mission hospital to carry their bag. The nurse asks her, “And you, Abena? When was your blood pressure last checked?” Abena laughs. “Me? I am only thirty. I am not sick.”

The nurse says, “Your mother has high blood pressure and your father has diabetes. These conditions run in families. Sit down. Let me check you.”

Abena’s pressure is 134 over 86. The nurse says, “It is not yet high. But it is close to the line. If you act now, it may never cross it.”

On the way home, Abena thinks about her brothers and sisters, and about Kwame. She asks herself, “Who else in our family should be checked?”

Ask the group.

  • Why did Abena think she did not need a check?
  • Who in your household has never had a blood pressure check?
  • What do people here say brings these conditions into a family?

Encourage discussion. Do not correct “wrong” answers. Let everyone give an opinion. This page is for discussion, not for teaching.

Say “Let us compare your ideas with the messages on the following pages.”

Picture 6.2Risks We Cannot Change and Risks We Can Change

Picture 6.2 · text sideRisks We Cannot Change and Risks We Can Change

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

Some risks we cannot change: growing older, and having these conditions in the family.

  • The chance grows as we grow older.
  • If a parent, a brother or a sister has high blood pressure or diabetes, your chance is higher.
  • A woman who had high blood pressure or high sugar during a pregnancy has a higher chance later in life.
B

Many risks we can change: too much salt, sugar and oil; too little movement; too much weight around the belly.

  • Too much salt raises blood pressure.
  • Sweet drinks and too much food add weight. Weight around the belly raises the chance of both conditions.
  • Sitting for most of the day raises the chance.
C

Tobacco and too much alcohol also raise the risk.

  • Tobacco damages the blood vessels.
  • Too much alcohol raises blood pressure.

Ask the group.

  • Which of these risks are in your household?
  • Which one could your household change first?
Additional information for the facilitator

Sources. For high blood pressure, the World Health Organization lists these risks that can be changed: too much salt, food high in fat, too few fruits and vegetables, too little physical activity, tobacco, alcohol and being overweight. It lists family history and older age among the risks that cannot be changed. For the common kind of diabetes, it lists being overweight, too little exercise and family history.

No blame. A risk is a chance, not a fault. Some people with none of these risks still get the conditions, and some people with many risks do not.

Later lessons. Lessons 7 to 12 cover food. Lesson 13 covers movement, Lesson 14 a healthy weight, Lesson 15 alcohol and tobacco, and Lesson 16 stress and sleep.

Picture 6.3Protect the Whole Household

Picture 6.3 · text sideProtect the Whole Household

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

Every adult in the household should have a blood pressure check at least once a year.

  • Take one adult from your household with you to your next clinic visit, or to a free check in the community.
  • Ask the health worker whether they also need a sugar check. People aged 40 or more, people with a big belly and people with diabetes in the family need one.
  • A person who is found early can start the Four Helpers before any harm is done.
B

The Four Helpers protect the whole family, including the children.

  • The same food and movement that control these conditions also help to prevent them.
  • Children learn their habits at home. What Kwame eats and does now will protect him as a man.
C

If your numbers are close to the line, act now.

  • Abena’s pressure was close to the line. She now uses less salt, drinks water in place of sweet drinks and walks every morning.
  • She will go for another check when the health worker tells her to.

Ask the group.

  • Which adult in your household will you take for a check first?
  • What can your household do together, starting this week?
Additional information for the facilitator

How often. Confirm the schedule for checks with the Ghana Health Service and the facility. International guidance commonly advises a blood pressure check for every adult at least once a year, and a sugar test for adults aged 40 or more and for younger adults with risks such as a big belly, high blood pressure or diabetes in the family.

Where to go. Name the places in the project area where adults who do not have the conditions can be checked free or at low cost.

Telling the family. Some participants have not told their relatives that they have high blood pressure or diabetes. Do not press them. Explain that telling brothers, sisters and grown children gives those relatives a reason to be checked.
